title: King John Seals Magna Carta
text:
By 1215 King John of England had lost most of his family's lands in France, including Normandy, and his attempt to win them back had ended in defeat at Bouvines in 1214. To pay for his wars he had squeezed his barons with heavy taxes, arbitrary fines and seizures, and he used the courts and hostages to keep them in line.

In the spring of 1215 a group of barons rebelled and took control of London. John was forced to negotiate. On June 15, 1215, at Runnymede, a meadow by the Thames near Windsor, he accepted the terms of a charter worked out with the help of Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury.

The charter dealt with many specific grievances, about inheritance, widows, debts and forests. But some clauses reached further. No free man was to be arrested, imprisoned, stripped of his rights or property, or outlawed except by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land. To no one would the king sell, deny or delay justice. A council of twenty-five barons was to enforce the charter.

The peace did not last. Within weeks John asked Pope Innocent III to annul the charter, which he did in August, and civil war followed. But after John's death in 1216 the charter was reissued in revised form, and it became a lasting foundation of the idea that rulers are bound by law.
lesson: Power used without limits tends to provoke the limits it tried to avoid. Rules that bind leaders protect everyone, including the leaders.
people: King John, the barons, Stephen Langton
source: Magna Carta (1215), clauses 39, 40 and 61; contemporary chroniclers including Roger of Wendover
